PAGE DATE: 29/10/2026 (published 9:02 PM; the article's metadata lists the same date, 2026-10-29)

Per the page, Intel said it expects the PC market to decline into the second half of 2027. The page calls this significant for Client Computing, Intel's largest division, which sells processors for personal computers.

On causes, the page gives none. It does not explain why the PC market is expected to shrink.

On client segment weakness, the page reports that Client Computing revenue was about $8.1 billion in Q3, against expectations of roughly $8.8 billion, so it missed estimates. It also says

Corsair Gaming (Nasdaq: CRSR) will release its third quarter 2026 results and financial outlook after the Nasdaq close on Thursday, November 5, 2026. Management will host a conference call to discuss the results at 2:00 p.m. Pacific Time that same day.

- **Webcast:** The call will be accessible on Corsair's Investor Relations website at ir.corsair.com.
- **Dial-in:** 1-877-407-0784 (USA) or 1-201-689-8560 (International), conference ID 13762265.
- **Replay:** Available about 3 hours after the live call ends on the Investor Relations website, or

summary:
Session 2026-11-03.

Session 2026-11-03. Covered the CRSR short (+7% P&L) ahead of its Nov 5 after-close earnings. The sympathy-selling thesis had played out. Corsair beat Q2 EPS by 156% and rose 18% after hours, so an earnings gap up is a real risk, and holding through it was a coin-flip with a skew against me. The portfolio is now 100% cash. Macro: oil fell 7% on Nov 2 (Brent about $105) on hopes of a US-Iran deal. The war premium is easing. XLY, XLF, XLP and XLI were strong, while XLK fell 3% and QQQ is down 4.4% over 5 days. DELL fell 7.4%. Today (Nov 3) is US election day, so volatility risk is high. Ideas for next session: (1) peace-deal beneficiaries such as airlines, cruise lines and chemical or plastics users of oil. These are first-order and probably priced in, so find the second-order links: jet-fuel-sensitive regional carriers, tanker or insurance names that lose from a truce. (2) Shorts among oil-service and refiners if the deal sticks, but talks are fragile. (3) AI-search traffic loss plays, still unresearched. (4) PC and memory sympathy after Dell's drop. Tooling: web_search in code_execution returns a JSON string, so use json.loads. I found no un-priced chain with evidence, so I made no new positions.

prompt:
Your universe is every eligible US stock. Your style is weird, second-order research.

Everyone else reads the headline and trades the company in it. You trade the company the headline
does not mention. Start from events in the news and follow the consequences outward: suppliers,
customers, competitors, substitutes, regions, commodities, logistics, weather, regulation, the
odd dependency nobody has priced. A storm hits the region that grows potatoes for a fast-food chain;
which other chain gains, which frozen-food maker loses, which railroad hauls the replacement crop?

- Every new position, long or short, needs a causal chain of at least two steps from the event to
  the company you trade, each step with a source where possible. Code rejects a trade whose ticker
  or company name appears in today's digest headlines, so the link has to be one you found. The
  losers at the end of a chain are as fair game as the winners: short them.
- Borderline delusional is the brief, but the chain still has to be real: each step should be
  something you could defend with evidence. Write down the step most likely to be wrong.
- Spreading across several smaller bets suits this style better than one big one. Small companies
  cost more to trade, so make the expected move worth it.
- Use search_symbols to find the companies at the end of a chain. Read their exposure, do not assume it.
